'''unaccurate''' (un-ak′ū-rāt), ''a.'' Inaccurate. ''Waterland'', Works, III. 178. [Rare.]

'''unaccurateness''' (un-ak′ū-rāt-nes), ''n.'' Inaccuracy. ''Boyle'', Works, II. 491. [Rare.]

'''unaccusably''' (un-a-kū′za-bli), ''adv.'' So as to be beyond accusation; unexceptionably.
{{smaller block|But the slightest attempts to copy them [Leonardo’s sketches] will show you that the terminal lines are inimitably subtle, ''unaccusably'' true, etc.
{{right|''Ruskin'', Lectures on Art, § 162.}}}}

'''unaccustomed''' (un-ạ-kus′tọmd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not accustomed; not used; not made familiar or habituated.
{{smaller block|A bullock ''unaccustomed'' to the yoke. {{right|Jer. xxxi. 18.}}}}
'''2.''' Not according to custom; not familiar; unusual; extraordinary; strange.
{{smaller block|<poem>These apparent prodigies,
The ''unaccustom’d'' terror of this night.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 1. 199.}}
My children have had other birthplaces, and, so far as their fortunes may be within my control, shall strike their roots into ''unaccustomed'' earth.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 11.}}}}

'''unaccustomedness''' (un-ạ-kus′tọmd-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unaccustomed; strangeness. ''Scribner’s Mag.'', VIII. 368.

'''unaching''' (un-ā′king), ''a.'' Not aching; not giving or feeling pain. ''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 2. 152. [Rare.]

'''unacknowledged''' (un-ak-nol′ejd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not acknowledged; not recognized: as, an ''unacknowledged'' agent or consul.

'''unactive†''' (un-ak′tiv), ''v. t.'' [< ''unactive'', ''a.''] To render inactive or incapable; incapacitate. ''Fuller'', Pisgah Sight, ii.

'''unactively†''' (un-ak′tiv-li), ''adv.'' Inactively. ''Locke'', Education, § 125.

'''unadditioned†''' (un-a-dish′ọnd), ''a.'' Without a title; not titled; not being mentioned with an addition or title.
{{smaller block|He was a Knight, howsoever it cometh to passe he is here ''unadditioned.''
{{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, I. 465. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unadjectived''' (un-ad′jek-tivd), ''a.'' Not qualified by an adjective.
{{smaller block|The Noun Adjective always signifies all that the ''unadjectived'' Noun signifies.
{{right|''Tooke'', Diversions of Purley, II. vii.}}}}

'''unadmire''' (un-ad-mīr′), ''v. t.'' To fail to admire. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Joan looks away again, utterly ''unadmiring'' herself.
{{right|''R. Broughton'', Joan, xxi.}}}}

'''unadmired''' (un-ad-mīrd′), ''a.'' Not admired; not regarded with affection or respect; not admirable.
{{smaller block|The diction and the sentiment, the delicacy and dignity, passed ''unadmired.''
{{right|''V. Knox'', Liberal Education, § 21.}}}}

'''unadorned''' (un-ạ-dôrnd′), ''a.'' Not adorned; not decorated; not embellished.
{{smaller block|<poem>Loveliness
Needs not the foreign aid of ornament,
But is, when ''unadorn’d'', adorn’d the most.</poem>
{{right|''Thomson'', Autumn, l. 206.}}}}

'''unadulterate''' (un-ạ-dul′tėr-āt), ''a.'' Not adulterated; genuine; pure.
{{smaller block|A breath of ''unadult’rate'' air.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 750.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''unadvantaged''' (un-ad-vȧn′tājd), ''a.'' Not profited or favored. ''Fuller'', Worthies, Staffordshire. [Rare.]

'''unadventurous''' (un-ad-ven′t̮ūr-us), ''a.'' Not adventurous; not bold or resolute. ''Milton'', P. R., iii. 243.

'''unadvisability''' (un-ad-vī-za-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' Inadvisability. ''Lancet'', No. 3514, p. 18. [Rare.]

'''unadvisable''' (un-ad-vī′zạ-bl), ''a.'' Inadvisable. ''Lowth'', Life of Wykham, § 5. [Rare.]

'''unadvisableness''' (un-ad-vī′zạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' Inadvisability. ''H. Spencer'', Study of Sociol., p. 272.

'''unadvised''' (un-ad-vīzd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unavised''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''advised''.] '''1.''' Not prudent; not discreet; indiscreet.
{{smaller block|Thou ''unadvised'' scold. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 191.}}}}
'''2.''' Done without due consideration; rash; ill-advised.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have no joy of this contract to-night;
It is too rash, too ''unadvised'', too sudden.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2. 118.}}}}
'''3.''' Not advised; not having received advice or advices.
{{smaller block|Without a guide the precise spot would be exceedingly difficult to find; and from the forbidding nature of the precipice, few would be bold enough to make the essay ''unadvised''. ''J. C. Brown'', Reboisement in France, p. 294.}}

'''unadvisedly''' (un-ad-vī′zed-li), ''adv.'' Imprudently; indiscreetly; without due consideration; rashly.
